analysis.one_liner: Requires construction sites to have certified safety specialists, written safety plans, faster accident reporting, and tougher criminal penalties for willful violations.
analysis.headline: The Senate Labor Committee reported the bill favorably in October 1990 and placed it on the Senate calendar, but no senator ever voted on it before that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have built a dedicated construction-safety arm inside OSHA: a new Office of Construction Safety, Health, and Education with extra inspectors who focus on the most dangerous sites. It would have required every covered construction contractor to maintain a written safety program, a site-specific safety plan, and a trained, certified safety specialist with the power to stop work in the face of imminent danger. It would also have required quick reporting of deaths, serious injuries, and structural failures, mandatory government inspections within 24 hours, and prison terms of up to 10 years — 20 for repeat offenders — for employers whose willful violations kill or seriously injure workers.
analysis.who_benefits: Construction workers, who face some of the highest fatality and serious-injury rates of any industry. The bill targets enforcement at worksites with a high potential for fatalities, gives workers a right to request written evaluations of hazards they perceive, and puts a trained safety professional with stop-work authority on covered sites.

how_it_helps.text: Establishes an Office of Construction Safety, Health, and Education within OSHA, directed to employ additional inspectors and concentrate enforcement on worksites with a high potential for fatalities or serious injuries.

Requires contractors to adopt written safety and health programs with regular inspections, emergency plans, safety training, and a procedure letting employees request a written evaluation of a perceived hazard.

Requires an onsite project safety plan with a hazard analysis and a construction process plan covering structural stability, and empowers a construction safety specialist to order hazards eliminated and to stop work when imminent danger exists.
Requires reporting of fatalities, serious injuries, and structural failures within 24 hours, with an OSHA site inspection within 24 hours and a public narrative description of what happened.
Raises criminal penalties so an employer whose willful violation causes a worker's death faces up to 10 years in prison, and up to 20 years after a prior conviction.

Creates a Construction Safety and Health Training Academy in OSHA to train inspectors and certify safety specialists, and requires specialists to complete a 40-hour safety course plus supervised on-the-job training.

analysis.who_pays: Construction contractors and project owners, who would bear the cost of hiring certified safety specialists, maintaining written plans and records, and meeting training and reporting requirements — costs likely passed into project prices, including for small contractors (the bill provides exemptions where requirements are not feasible and a small-business liaison to help firms comply).

drawbacks.text: Compliance would add real costs for contractors — certified specialists on covered sites, written plans, training, and detailed recordkeeping — with the heaviest relative burden on small firms, which the bill acknowledges through its small-business liaison and limited exemption authority.

The specialist certification regime (40-hour course plus at least 18 months of supervised on-the-job training) could be slow to scale, potentially delaying projects while enough certified specialists are trained.

The bill layers new planning, notice, and reporting duties on top of existing OSHA rules, adding federal paperwork and inspection priorities that contractors argued were duplicative; minority views were filed when the committee reported it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core tradeoff is real: worker lives versus compliance costs in a dangerous industry. The bill was drafted to soften the cost side — inspection priorities weighted toward bad actors, a small-business liaison, feasibility exemptions, and regulations tailored to firms of different sizes — but a certified specialist on every covered site is a substantial, ongoing expense, especially for small contractors. For workers, the protections (hazard evaluations on request, stop-work authority, 24-hour inspections after serious incidents, and prison exposure for willful violations) are meaningful and targeted at the deadliest risks.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Labor Committee approved the bill and placed it on the Senate calendar in late 1990, but Senate leadership never brought it up for a vote, and the bill died when the 101st Congress ended in January 1991 without ever reaching the House.

narrative.text: Sen. Christopher Dodd introduced the bill with Sen. Joseph Lieberman on May 4, 1989, and it was referred to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources.
The committee held hearings in November 1989 and ordered the bill reported favorably with a substitute amendment on September 26, 1990.
On October 27, 1990, Senator Kennedy reported the bill to the Senate with an amendment in the nature of a substitute, with minority views filed.

The bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 1028) but received no further action; no floor vote ever occurred and the House never considered it before the Congress ended January 3, 1991.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Construction contractors and project owners are better off: no certified-specialist requirement, no mandatory site safety plans, no 24-hour serious-injury reporting, and no enhanced criminal penalties took effect. Construction workers continue to face the risks the bill was written to reduce.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had only Democratic cosponsors and a Democratic committee chair reported it, but it cleared committee with minority views filed and no recorded floor vote, so the partisan split at the end is not fully documented.

industries.note: The bill would have required certified safety specialists, written safety programs, site-specific plans, and 24-hour accident reporting on covered projects, with criminal exposure for willful violations that kill or injure workers. Their compliance costs rise precisely where worker protections are added.

Owners would have faced priority inspections keyed to their projects' injury and severity rates and constructor-designation duties, and could not be excluded from inspections. Costs would likely be passed through to project budgets.

The bill creates a federal training academy and a certification requirement for construction safety specialists, opening a market for safety training courses and cooperative agreements with educational institutions.

industries.industry: Federal safety agencies (OSHA and state safety programs)
industries.note: OSHA would gain a dedicated construction office, additional inspectors, and a training academy, with federal grants to states to administer and enforce the new requirements.
